aurora.overview: A lighting treatment built from broad, luminous color fields. It supplies atmosphere behind an interface rather than a navigation model.
steps: Keep the gradient behind the header
Put body text on an opaque panel
Use one accent for the primary action
aurora.avoid: Animating the entire background or placing small text over changing colors.
aurora.example: A music discovery page with an aurora header and solid album rows.
aurora.typeAdvice: Use a medium-weight sans-serif. Keep luminous effects off the letterforms.
aurora.referenceNote: Look at the large blue light fields and soft-edged color transitions. These poster treatments suggest atmosphere; they do not demonstrate a complete interface.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

pixel-art.overview: An image-making approach where the placement of individual pixels is visible and deliberate. Pixel illustration does not require pixel-sized interface controls.
steps: Draw icons on a consistent source grid
Scale artwork by whole-number multiples
Pair display lettering with normal body text
pixel-art.avoid: Blurry scaling, tiny bitmap paragraphs, or controls whose hit areas are only as large as their sprites.
pixel-art.example: A game library with pixel cover art and readable save-file details.
pixel-art.typeAdvice: A bitmap display face can work for a short title; use a normal-width monospace or sans-serif for descriptions.
pixel-art.referenceNote: Compare the deliberately stepped silhouettes and limited colors. Some tiles are broader retro illustration references, so inspect the pixel construction rather than assuming every tile uses the same technique.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

japandi.overview: A contemporary interiors-inspired blend of restrained Japanese and Scandinavian references. For screens, the useful translation is material warmth and economical composition.
steps: Use one quiet surface color
Align content to a simple grid
Make product photography carry the texture
japandi.avoid: Treating beige as the whole concept or reducing text contrast to create calm.
japandi.example: A furniture catalog with oak photography, generous gutters, and direct product information.
japandi.typeAdvice: Choose an understated sans-serif with open counters. Avoid excessive tracking in body copy.
japandi.referenceNote: Notice the warm paper tones, simplified objects, and generous margins. The board is an interiors-and-print interpretation rather than an example of Japanese interface conventions.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

bauhaus.overview: A modern screen interpretation of the Bauhaus school, which operated from 1919 to 1933. Geometric studies are a useful reference, but red-yellow-blue graphics are only one part of its varied output.
steps: Use a modular grid
Let one geometric form anchor the composition
Assign primary colors distinct visual roles
bauhaus.avoid: Reducing the school to decorative circles or claiming every Bauhaus work rejected ornament in the same way.
bauhaus.example: An exhibition index with a geometric title panel and disciplined event rows.
bauhaus.typeAdvice: Use a geometric sans-serif for display and a readable sans-serif for details; geometry should not distort long text.
bauhaus.referenceNote: Compare the geometric balance, color blocks, and directional lettering. These are contemporary poster references, not a catalog of original Bauhaus works.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

brutalism.overview: A web approach that exposes structure through plain typography, hard boundaries, and direct links. Its architectural namesake is an analogy, not a prescription for bad usability.
steps: Use explicit link text
Separate sections with rules
Make every action respond immediately
brutalism.avoid: Confusing deliberate roughness with broken navigation, tiny text, or inaccessible contrast.
brutalism.example: A project archive with oversized titles, underlined links, and no entrance sequence.
brutalism.typeAdvice: System sans-serif or monospace works well. Large size and explicit links matter more than a novelty font.
brutalism.referenceNote: The board combines architectural imagery and forceful print typography. Translate its visible structure into web layout; a concrete building photograph alone does not demonstrate web brutalism.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

bento-box.overview: A layout pattern using differently sized cards within a shared grid. The hierarchy comes from card size and grouping rather than from a particular color palette.
steps: Choose one lead card
Give each card a single purpose
Define the mobile reading order before adding spans
bento-box.avoid: Making everything a card, cropping essential content to fixed heights, or changing the reading order on mobile.
bento-box.example: A product overview with one demonstration, two capabilities, and a compact release note.
bento-box.typeAdvice: Keep one sans-serif family across cards. Use size and weight to distinguish the lead card from supporting information.
bento-box.referenceNote: Notice how different image and text blocks fit a shared grid. Check which block leads each composition and how the smaller blocks support it.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

utilitarian.overview: A task-oriented approach that makes information easy to compare and actions easy to repeat. Density is useful only when it reduces work for the reader.
steps: Align numbers and show units
Keep filters near the results
Use status text alongside color
utilitarian.avoid: Hiding important actions in icon-only menus or showing more metrics than a decision needs.
utilitarian.example: An operations queue with owner, state, age, and one clear next action per row.
utilitarian.typeAdvice: Use a legible sans-serif and tabular numerals for comparable values. Reserve monospace for identifiers.
utilitarian.referenceNote: The examples use restrained grids, alignment, and clear numerical detail. They are mostly graphic layouts; a useful operational interface also needs task-specific information and controls.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

neo-frutiger-aero.overview: A contemporary revival of glossy, nature-and-technology imagery associated with Frutiger Aero. This is a visual vocabulary, not a native operating-system specification.
steps: Use one environmental illustration
Add restrained highlights to prominent controls
Keep content surfaces stable and readable
neo-frutiger-aero.avoid: Assuming every glossy interface belongs to the same movement or adding reflective effects to every element.
neo-frutiger-aero.example: A weather concept with sky imagery and a solid forecast table.
neo-frutiger-aero.typeAdvice: Use a humanist sans-serif with open shapes. Gloss belongs to surfaces rather than text.
neo-frutiger-aero.referenceNote: Look for the glossy blue forms, green landscapes, and bright skies. The shared cue is optimistic nature-and-technology imagery rather than a single operating system.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

glassmorphism.overview: A surface treatment that suggests frosted glass through translucency, blur, and a visible edge. Its success depends on what is behind the surface.
steps: Use glass for a small overlay or toolbar
Provide an opaque fallback
Test text over the lightest and darkest background regions
glassmorphism.avoid: Stacking many blurred layers or assuming blur automatically supplies enough contrast.
glassmorphism.example: A photo viewer with one translucent toolbar and opaque menus.
glassmorphism.typeAdvice: Use medium-weight text on translucent surfaces. Thin strokes are vulnerable to changing backgrounds.
glassmorphism.referenceNote: The board includes glass-like distortion and refracted print effects. Those are related material references, but not all demonstrate the frosted, blurred surface used in interface glassmorphism.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

neo-brutalism.overview: A contemporary web treatment combining assertive borders, flat color, and hard offset shadows. Its visual weight comes from outlines, spacing, and sharply separated color areas.
steps: Choose a consistent border weight
Use a hard shadow to signal elevation
Keep labels literal and states distinct
neo-brutalism.avoid: Copying one brand as the definition of the style or using hard shadows on noninteractive decoration indiscriminately.
neo-brutalism.example: A workshop registration page with outlined tickets and a high-contrast booking button.
neo-brutalism.typeAdvice: Use assertive sans-serif headings with plain sentence-case control labels. Borders already provide emphasis.
neo-brutalism.referenceNote: Look at the black outlines, flat fills, and offset panel shapes. Several examples use playful pastel color, showing why orange is not a required palette.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

luxury-typography.overview: An editorial treatment in which proportion, type detail, and spacing carry most of the identity. It does not require microscopic text or excessive empty space.
steps: Use a high-contrast serif only at display sizes
Keep body copy in a sturdier face
Reserve tracked capitals for short labels
luxury-typography.avoid: Thin strokes at small sizes, extreme tracking in paragraphs, or making price and availability difficult to find.
luxury-typography.example: A small jewelry catalog with large product names and plainly stated materials and prices.
luxury-typography.typeAdvice: Try a high-contrast display serif such as Playfair Display for headings, paired with a sturdier reading face.
luxury-typography.referenceNote: Notice how the serif titles, material photography, and restrained copy work together. The surrounding space gives the type emphasis without requiring every label to be small.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

memphis.overview: A graphic interpretation of the Memphis design group's playful clashes of shape, pattern, and color. It is intentionally more unruly than a modernist geometric system.
steps: Choose a limited set of patterns
Place them in margins or illustration
Keep the reading area comparatively quiet
memphis.avoid: Putting competing patterns behind text or treating every bright geometric layout as Memphis.
memphis.example: A festival program with patterned section dividers and clean schedule cards.
memphis.typeAdvice: Bold geometric sans-serif lettering complements the shapes. Keep body text free of pattern and rotation.
memphis.referenceNote: Compare the patterned fields, clashing shapes, and deliberately playful compositions. The references are modern graphics drawing on the vocabulary of the design group.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

art-deco.overview: A decorative vocabulary of stepped geometry, symmetry, and stylized luxury. Its screen adaptation works best as a frame around content rather than an all-over effect.
steps: Build a symmetrical title composition
Use metallic color as a flat accent
Pair a decorative heading with restrained body text
art-deco.avoid: Gold-on-gold text, excessive hairlines, or substituting generic luxury styling for the geometric structure.
art-deco.example: A cinema program with stepped borders and a clear screening schedule.
art-deco.typeAdvice: Use short geometric display lettering, with controlled symmetry. A neutral body face prevents the page becoming a poster at every scale.
art-deco.referenceNote: Look for stepped borders, symmetrical framing, and geometric lettering. The metallic-looking accents reinforce the structure rather than defining it by themselves.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

pop-art.overview: An approach that draws on commercial imagery and popular culture. Repetition, enlarged everyday objects, and comic-print devices are possible techniques, not universal requirements.
steps: Choose one recognizable everyday subject
Use repeated panels deliberately
Keep halftone away from small labels
pop-art.avoid: Reducing the movement to comic dots or using copyrighted characters without considering their source.
pop-art.example: A cultural magazine cover with repeated object photography and a plain article index.
pop-art.typeAdvice: Try heavy condensed headlines. Comic lettering should remain a deliberate reference rather than the default for all text.
pop-art.referenceNote: The board mixes bold commercial lettering, comic imagery, and repeated graphic devices. These are contemporary popular-culture references rather than a survey of the historical movement.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

mid-century.overview: A screen interpretation of mid-century modern graphics and objects: economical forms, warm materials, and playful but controlled abstraction.
steps: Pair one organic shape with a clear grid
Use muted colors with a darker text anchor
Choose a small family of repeatable motifs
mid-century.avoid: Turning every section into a retro poster or using period decoration where users need precise controls.
mid-century.example: A homewares catalog with abstract shapes around straightforward product photography.
mid-century.typeAdvice: A geometric sans-serif or warm editorial serif can work. Let the illustration decide which feels coherent.
mid-century.referenceNote: Compare the flattened organic shapes and economical color combinations. The figures and abstract forms remain readable because the compositions use a few strong relationships.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

modular-typography.overview: A lettering approach built from repeated geometric units. The system is in the construction of the letters, not simply in using a grid for page layout.
steps: Define a small set of strokes or tiles
Use constructed lettering for short headings
Use a conventional face for reading and controls
modular-typography.avoid: Forcing modular display letters into paragraphs or calling any sans-serif grid layout modular typography.
modular-typography.example: An exhibition identity whose title is constructed from repeatable tiles above a readable program.
modular-typography.typeAdvice: Construct a title from repeated units, then use a conventional text face below it. Show the module if construction is the subject.
modular-typography.referenceNote: Look at the repeated shapes and constructed letter parts. A grid is only the starting point: the defining question is whether the letterforms share a repeatable module.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

retro-y2k.overview: A contemporary reading of late-1990s and early-2000s digital futurism. Chrome, translucent plastics, and inflated forms distinguish it from a 1980s synthwave scene.
steps: Choose one metallic focal object
Pair experimental display type with simple labels
Use a limited bright accent palette
retro-y2k.avoid: Mixing every retro decade together or applying metallic gradients to body text.
retro-y2k.example: A music release page with a chrome title object and simple track listings.
retro-y2k.typeAdvice: Extended or rounded display lettering can supply the period reference. Keep chrome out of body text.
retro-y2k.referenceNote: Notice the metallic objects, translucent forms, and shiny digital surfaces. The board mixes millennium-era references with later revival graphics.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

cybercore.overview: A broad internet aesthetic drawing on fictional hacker interfaces and digital dystopia. It is expressive fiction, not evidence that a product is technically sophisticated.
steps: Use monospace for actual structured information
Keep glitch effects in static artwork
Give real system states explicit labels
cybercore.avoid: Fake telemetry, flashing warnings, or presenting decorative code as real diagnostic data.
cybercore.example: A fiction anthology with terminal-inspired chapter labels and normal reading typography.
cybercore.typeAdvice: Use monospace for structured labels and a simple sans-serif for longer reading. Do not replace letters with unreadable symbols.
cybercore.referenceNote: Look at the metallic lettering, dark surfaces, and electric purple-blue accents. These are fictional digital moods, not demonstrations of actual cybersecurity tools.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

synthwave.overview: A retro-futurist visual vocabulary associated with synthwave music, drawing heavily on imagined 1980s nightscapes. It differs from vaporwave's collage and corporate nostalgia.
steps: Keep the horizon in an illustration
Choose two neon accents
Use a dark solid surface for track and event details
synthwave.avoid: Continuous glowing animation, unreadable outlined text, or calling it an original 1980s interface standard.
synthwave.example: A concert page with a sunset poster and a clean date-and-ticket panel.
synthwave.typeAdvice: An italic or angular display title can suggest speed. Use solid, unglowing text for event details.
synthwave.referenceNote: The board includes sunset, palm, neon, and retro display cues. Separate the imagined 1980s atmosphere from the more recent music and graphic culture using it.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

vaporwave.overview: An internet-era collage aesthetic associated with vaporwave music, combining commercial nostalgia, surreal space, and degraded digital media. Its tone can be ambiguous rather than purely celebratory.
steps: Compose one deliberate collage
Use degraded texture as an image layer
Keep navigation outside the distortion
vaporwave.avoid: Random Japanese text as decoration, inaccessible glitch effects, or assuming every work makes the same political argument.
vaporwave.example: An album archive with a surreal cover collage and plainly labeled listening links.
vaporwave.typeAdvice: Monospace and restrained system typography can reference older software. Use meaningful language rather than decorative foreign glyphs.
vaporwave.referenceNote: Compare the pastel-neon collage, floating objects, and artificial spatial depth. The examples emphasize a contemporary commercial interpretation of the mood.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

coquette.overview: A contemporary romantic aesthetic using bows, lace, soft colors, and intimate decorative details. Those visual choices do not define the gender or personality of the audience.
steps: Use one ribbon or border motif
Keep text darker than the pastel surface
Reserve script lettering for a short accent
coquette.avoid: Gendered assumptions, unreadable script, or decorative flourishes crowding controls.
coquette.example: A stationery collection with ribbon photography and straightforward product descriptions.
coquette.typeAdvice: A restrained serif with an optional short script accent works. Use plain typography for prices and controls.
coquette.referenceNote: Look at the romantic lettering, pink palette, and soft decorative details. Some examples overlap with broader beauty and fashion branding rather than showing a sharply bounded style.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

dark-academia.overview: A contemporary scholarly mood using dark wood, books, archival imagery, and subdued light. Occult and fantasy motifs are optional variants, not the definition of academia.
steps: Use a sturdy serif for titles
Show real bibliographic or collection details
Keep the reading surface lighter or the text strongly contrasted
dark-academia.avoid: Equating scholarship with occult imagery or making a dark page difficult to read.
dark-academia.example: A reading journal with book details, dated notes, and a restrained library palette.
dark-academia.typeAdvice: A sturdy book serif suits titles and reading. Keep blackletter or occult display lettering out of ordinary paragraphs.
dark-academia.referenceNote: The references include book covers, shadowed architecture, and fantasy imagery. The fantasy elements are one variation; a reading journal can use the scholarly atmosphere without them.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

light-academia.overview: A contemporary scholarly mood centered on daylight, paper, and reflective reading. It shares the bookish cues of dark academia with a lighter tonal range.
steps: Use clear chapter headings
Limit the text measure
Pair warm surfaces with dark ink-colored text
light-academia.avoid: Faint beige text or decorative book imagery replacing useful information about the material.
light-academia.example: A literature notebook with quotations, sources, and spacious chapter navigation.
light-academia.typeAdvice: Use a bookish serif, comfortable line-height, and clear footnotes. A light palette is no reason for faint type.
light-academia.referenceNote: Notice the warm paper, classical image fragments, and bookish typography. Several examples overlap with religious or classical editorial graphics.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

anthropomorphic.overview: A character-based treatment that gives objects human expressions or behavior. It can add identity without pretending the interface has feelings or understands the user.
steps: Give the character a limited supporting role
Keep instructions explicit in text
Use the same expression consistently for the same state
anthropomorphic.avoid: Guilt-based reminders, emotional pressure, or mascots interrupting routine tasks.
anthropomorphic.example: A language exercise with a small character illustration beside a factual answer explanation.
anthropomorphic.typeAdvice: Use a friendly but conventional sans-serif. The character can express personality without turning every label into dialogue.
anthropomorphic.referenceNote: Look at how the illustrated objects gain expressions and gestures. Their personality is conveyed in the artwork, while the surrounding text can stay direct.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

bohemian.overview: An eclectic composition of natural texture, collected objects, and varied patterns. Specific references matter more than a generic claim of being global or exotic.
steps: Select patterns from identifiable sources
Balance a busy image with a quiet reading area
Use a repeated spacing system
bohemian.avoid: Treating distinct cultures as interchangeable decoration or making every layer compete for attention.
bohemian.example: An independent maker's catalog with credited textiles and direct descriptions of materials.
bohemian.typeAdvice: Use a warm serif or simple sans-serif to hold the layered imagery together. Limit the number of display treatments.
bohemian.referenceNote: The board emphasizes botanical shapes, earthy color, and contemporary lifestyle posters. It is a narrow graphic selection, not a representation of every tradition described as bohemian.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

shabby-chic.overview: An interiors-inspired treatment of weathered finishes, vintage florals, and soft color. On a screen, the worn effect belongs to imagery and framing rather than text clarity.
steps: Use distressing on a border or photo
Keep body type crisp
Repeat one floral motif sparingly
shabby-chic.avoid: Distressing the actual text, low-contrast pastel controls, or manufacturing age as a factual provenance claim.
shabby-chic.example: A vintage homewares listing with condition photographs and clearly labeled item details.
shabby-chic.typeAdvice: A serif with a short handwritten accent can establish the mood. Do not distress the text itself.
shabby-chic.referenceNote: Look for faded color, floral decoration, and nostalgic domestic imagery. Keep the weathering in the artwork while preserving crisp captions and controls.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

cottagecore.overview: A contemporary pastoral aesthetic of gardens, domestic craft, and rural imagery. It is a mood and storytelling vocabulary, not evidence of how an object was produced.
steps: Use real material or process photographs
Keep botanical framing outside the text
Let captions explain the pictured activity
cottagecore.avoid: Romantic imagery standing in for product facts or implying a handmade origin without support.
cottagecore.example: A gardening notebook with seasonal photographs, plant names, and practical observations.
cottagecore.typeAdvice: Use a readable serif for the journal voice and a plain face for plant names, dates, and instructions.
cottagecore.referenceNote: Notice the garden scenes, domestic objects, and handmade-looking illustration. Captions and practical details can make this imagery more than a general rural mood.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

wabi-sabi.overview: A Japanese aesthetic reference associated with transience, irregularity, and the character of materials. A restrained screen interpretation should not flatten that context into generic cozy branding.
steps: Use real texture with visible variation
Allow asymmetry in imagery
Keep navigation and text alignment dependable
wabi-sabi.avoid: Calling any beige interface wabi-sabi, treating kintsugi as its synonym, or simulating imperfection in functional controls.
wabi-sabi.example: A ceramics archive with close photographs of surfaces and concise notes about each object.

source.label: The Met: Japanese tea and material aesthetics

wabi-sabi.typeAdvice: A quiet serif or sans-serif can work. Irregular material photography supplies the character; imitation handwriting is unnecessary.
wabi-sabi.referenceNote: The board emphasizes quiet material imagery and restrained composition. These contemporary graphics are adjacent references; the tea-ceremony source provides more specific cultural context.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

neoclassical.overview: A visual reference to the ordered proportions and antique forms of Neoclassicism. A digital adaptation can borrow its symmetry without pretending a typeface is historically authentic.
steps: Center the main title sparingly
Use balanced margins and clear rules
Keep supporting text conventionally aligned
neoclassical.avoid: Treating all classical ornament as one period or centering long paragraphs for supposed elegance.
neoclassical.example: A museum collection page with a balanced introduction and a clear object catalog.
neoclassical.typeAdvice: Use carefully proportioned serif titles. Roman-style capitals are best kept to a short heading, not a paragraph.
neoclassical.referenceNote: The board mixes antique sculpture with contemporary dramatic poster design. Study the classical references while distinguishing them from an original Neoclassical composition.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

baroque.overview: A visual reference to dramatic movement, layered composition, and rich ornament in Baroque art. Its useful digital translation is controlled emphasis rather than maximum decoration everywhere.
steps: Choose one dominant image
Concentrate ornament around its frame
Let supporting information remain quiet
baroque.avoid: Making every component compete for drama or describing later typefaces as authentic Baroque typography.
baroque.example: An opera program with a dramatic production image and an uncomplicated booking panel.
baroque.typeAdvice: A rich serif display treatment can balance the imagery. This is a modern pairing, not a claim that the typeface dates to the Baroque period.
baroque.referenceNote: Look at the ornate frames and dense decorative edges. The board is useful for framing ideas but does not capture the full range of Baroque painting, architecture, and sculpture.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

victorian.overview: A broad reference to nineteenth-century British visual culture, which contained many competing revival styles. Ornate print is one useful source, not a single universal Victorian interface language.
steps: Use one period-inspired title treatment
Give metadata its own simple type style
Use ornament to mark sections
victorian.avoid: Stacking many novelty fonts or presenting the entire period as one dark, luxurious look.
victorian.example: A local-history exhibition page with a poster-like title and readable artifact captions.
victorian.typeAdvice: Try one slab-serif or ornamental headline. Pair it with a quiet reading face rather than a collection of competing period fonts.
victorian.referenceNote: Notice the layered borders, ornamental lettering, and printed ephemera. The examples are period-inspired graphics rather than proof of a single uniform Victorian style.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

art-nouveau.overview: A decorative approach associated with flowing lines and stylized natural forms across several media. The relationship between image, lettering, and border matters more than adding a floral icon.
steps: Draw one continuous framing motif
Keep display lettering short
Use plain body text inside the frame
art-nouveau.avoid: Generic flowers without the line structure or elaborate letterforms in controls and paragraphs.
art-nouveau.example: A botanical exhibition page whose border follows the composition of its main illustration.
art-nouveau.typeAdvice: Use organic display lettering for a short title. Keep the smaller text conventional so the border and lettering do not compete.
art-nouveau.referenceNote: Compare the continuous curves, botanical framing, and integrated figure-and-letter compositions. Those relationships are more distinctive than a floral motif on its own.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

gothic.overview: A modern graphic interpretation of Gothic architectural references, including pointed forms and tracery. Black palettes and occult motifs belong to some later reinterpretations, not all Gothic art.
steps: Use the arch as an image frame
Reserve blackletter for brief titles
Keep navigation in a highly legible face
gothic.avoid: Conflating medieval architecture, Gothic revival, and contemporary goth culture without explanation.
gothic.example: An architectural photo essay with arch-shaped images and clear historical captions.
gothic.typeAdvice: Blackletter may suit a short display title; use an open, readable serif or sans-serif for supporting text.
gothic.referenceNote: The board combines architecture, horror covers, and later goth-associated graphics. Use the distinction between medieval form and contemporary genre imagery when choosing a reference.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

steampunk.overview: A speculative genre combining historical industrial imagery with imagined technology. Gears and brass establish fiction; they should not obscure how a real interface works.
steps: Give decorative mechanisms a plausible visual role
Use a simple control layout
Separate fictional gauges from real data
steampunk.avoid: Random gears on every surface or unlabeled dials that imply nonexistent measurements.
steampunk.example: A fictional invention catalog with mechanical illustrations and readable specifications.
steampunk.typeAdvice: Slab-serif display lettering can reference industrial print. Monospace is useful for actual specifications, not ornamental pseudo-data.
steampunk.referenceNote: Look for invented machinery, antique print, and industrial fantasy. The examples are speculative genre graphics, not documentation of functioning historical devices.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

ethereal.overview: An atmospheric treatment using soft light, translucent imagery, and spacious composition. Softness belongs to the imagery; text and controls still need definite edges.
steps: Use a soft image as the focal point
Place reading text on a stable surface
Keep movement optional and minimal
ethereal.avoid: Using low contrast as the defining principle or making the cursor chase floating controls.
ethereal.example: A photography portfolio with luminous images and restrained, legible captions.
ethereal.typeAdvice: Use a clear serif or sans-serif at a comfortable weight. Avoid hairline strokes that vanish into luminous imagery.
ethereal.referenceNote: The board uses blur, luminous color, and softened image boundaries. Some tiles are darker and more energetic than a pastel interpretation, showing that light treatment matters more than hue alone.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

filigree.overview: A reference to delicate ornamental metalwork made from fine threads. In screen graphics, the useful feature is a coherent network of fine lines around a clear central subject.
steps: Use vector artwork for clean scaling
Keep detail away from small text
Reduce border complexity on narrow screens
filigree.avoid: Calling any flourish filigree or using hairline decoration as an essential control boundary.
filigree.example: A craft catalog with detailed object photographs and a fine ornamental heading frame.
filigree.typeAdvice: Pair ornate borders with a restrained serif. Do not add a second layer of flourishes to every letter.
filigree.referenceNote: Notice the fine ornamental lines framing the titles. These are graphic interpretations of ornamental craft; use the line rhythm without treating every flourish as literal metalwork.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

acanthus.overview: An ornamental reference to stylized acanthus foliage used in classical architectural decoration. It is a specific leaf-and-scroll vocabulary rather than a synonym for all botanical ornament.
steps: Choose a consistent leaf drawing
Use it at section openings
Leave content columns unornamented
acanthus.avoid: Mixing unrelated botanical motifs while labeling them acanthus or overwhelming small screens with borders.
acanthus.example: An architectural detail archive with close images and a restrained leaf divider.
acanthus.typeAdvice: A balanced serif works with classical leaf ornament. Keep title spacing measured rather than excessively wide.
acanthus.referenceNote: The board includes several kinds of botanical and classical ornament. Compare the leaf shapes carefully: not every floral border is an acanthus pattern.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

conceptual-sketch.overview: A deliberately unfinished visual treatment that makes ideas and relationships easy to discuss. Sketchiness can communicate a draft state, but should not conceal the status of real functionality.
steps: Use annotations to explain actual decisions
Keep labels typeset and readable
Mark unfinished or hypothetical features explicitly
conceptual-sketch.avoid: Presenting an incomplete workflow as working or making every line so irregular that relationships become ambiguous.
conceptual-sketch.example: A product concept page with an annotated flow and clearly marked open questions.
conceptual-sketch.typeAdvice: Use typeset annotations or highly legible handwriting. Labels should explain the diagram without requiring deciphering.
conceptual-sketch.referenceNote: Look at the loose drawings and informal annotations. Much of this board is finished poster art using sketch-like marks, which differs from an actual early-stage wireframe.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

tenebrism.overview: A dramatic lighting approach in which concentrated illumination emerges from extensive darkness. It is more specific than a dark theme or ordinary high-contrast text.
steps: Let one lit image establish the mood
Keep interface text evenly readable
Reserve darkness for framing rather than hiding controls
tenebrism.avoid: Equating any black background with tenebrism or obscuring navigation to create drama.
tenebrism.example: A portrait gallery with one illuminated subject and unobtrusive but visible metadata.
tenebrism.typeAdvice: Use solid, readable text beside the dramatic image. A serif can support the mood without needing a glow or shadow.
tenebrism.referenceNote: Notice how the faces and focal objects emerge from extensive shadow. These contemporary photographic compositions are lighting references, not historical paintings.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

pointillism.overview: An image-making technique using discrete dots of color. It is related to Divisionism, but the terms are not interchangeable: dots are a particular way of separating color.
steps: Use dots within illustration
Preview at actual display sizes
Preserve clean typography and controls
pointillism.avoid: Calling any dotted texture pointillism or using dense live particles where a static image would work.
pointillism.example: An art lesson showing a dotted image beside a zoomed detail and a readable explanation.
pointillism.typeAdvice: Use clean text as a contrast to the dotted illustration. Pixel fonts would imply a different construction method.
pointillism.referenceNote: This board mainly uses halftone and stippled print effects. Those are useful comparisons, but they do not demonstrate the color-separation technique of painted Pointillism; use the linked museum source for that distinction.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

mixed-media.overview: A composition combining distinct media such as photography, drawing, and cut paper. The contrast between the materials should contribute to the idea.
steps: Choose one dominant medium
Use the second to annotate or contrast
Repeat a small set of alignment points
mixed-media.avoid: Adding texture without purpose or letting overlaps cover text and links.
mixed-media.example: A project case study combining process photographs with drawn annotations.
mixed-media.typeAdvice: Choose one dependable reading family. A second display voice should correspond to a distinct layer or speaker.
mixed-media.referenceNote: Compare the photographs, cutout shapes, and drawn additions. The strongest combinations give the added layer a specific role rather than simply adding texture.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

surrealism.overview: An artistic and literary movement exploring the unconscious and unexpected associations. A screen interpretation can use impossible imagery while keeping the actual interaction understandable.
steps: Build one meaningful impossible scene
Keep navigation spatially stable
Use captions when the image needs context
surrealism.avoid: Random visual oddity without an idea or making essential actions behave unpredictably.
surrealism.example: A literary journal with a surreal cover image and conventional article navigation.
surrealism.typeAdvice: Conventional typography can make the impossible image more striking. Distort a title only when the distortion carries an idea.
surrealism.referenceNote: Look at the altered scale, improbable objects, and impossible spatial relationships. These are contemporary graphic interpretations of surreal imagery.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

mystical-western.overview: A contemporary hybrid of desert imagery, Western lettering, and celestial or occult motifs. It is a constructed mood, not a single historical tradition.
steps: Choose one landscape and one symbol family
Use display lettering only for titles
Explain symbols when they carry meaning
mystical-western.avoid: Treating sacred imagery as interchangeable decoration or asserting a shared cultural origin for the whole blend.
mystical-western.example: A fictional desert festival poster with a readable itinerary and location details.
mystical-western.typeAdvice: A short Western display title can establish the genre. Use a conventional serif for the itinerary or story.
mystical-western.referenceNote: The board mixes desert scenes, celestial imagery, and ornamental framing. It illustrates the hybrid mood rather than one historical or cultural tradition.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

kitsch.overview: A treatment of excess, sentimentality, and conspicuous ornament that can be affectionate, ironic, or both. Its effect depends on the subject and audience.
steps: Pick a clear theme for the excess
Keep one stable content grid
Let the joke live in imagery and headlines
kitsch.avoid: Assuming irony is obvious or making the actual transaction confusing as part of the joke.
kitsch.example: A novelty object collection with exuberant imagery and clear catalog information.
kitsch.typeAdvice: Choose one exuberant display face and a plain supporting face. Deliberate excess still benefits from hierarchy.
kitsch.referenceNote: Notice the exaggerated objects, conspicuous lettering, and cheerful excess. The compositions share an attitude more than a consistent type or color system.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

graffiti.overview: A reference to lettering and mark-making in public space, with varied practices and local histories. A spray texture alone does not convey the structure or authorship of a piece.
steps: Use original or credited artwork
Keep expressive lettering in large images
Typeset dates, locations, and controls plainly
graffiti.avoid: Treating all street art as one style or using an artist's work as anonymous background texture.
graffiti.example: An artist portfolio showing complete works, detail images, and credited locations.
graffiti.typeAdvice: Let original lettering remain artwork. Typeset its title, creator, and details in a separate, readable voice.
graffiti.referenceNote: Compare the expressive letter shapes, outlines, and layered marks. Treat individual pieces as authored artwork rather than anonymous background texture.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

scrapbook.overview: A composition that organizes photographs, notes, and keepsakes as a personal record. It becomes useful when the layering helps connect an image to its story.
steps: Pair every image with nearby context
Limit rotation to decoration
Keep the reading order explicit
scrapbook.avoid: Scattering captions away from photos or turning chronology into a puzzle.
scrapbook.example: A yearly journal with dated photo groups and short notes beside each event.
scrapbook.typeAdvice: Use a readable serif for the story and a limited handwriting accent for personal notes. Dates should be easy to scan.
scrapbook.referenceNote: The board layers cutouts, paper fragments, and handwritten-looking notes. A personal timeline can borrow the material relationships while keeping dates and captions orderly.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

southwest.overview: A regional visual reference to desert landscapes and locally specific craft and architecture. The region contains distinct living cultures; this guide uses landscape color rather than claiming a universal cultural pattern.
steps: Start with an identifiable place
Credit any craft or pattern source
Use landscape photography and plain geographic labels
southwest.avoid: Combining Indigenous motifs indiscriminately or describing a contemporary community only as a historical influence.
southwest.example: A desert travel journal with place names, terrain photographs, and credited local work.
southwest.typeAdvice: A clear sans-serif lets place and material photography speak. Avoid generic novelty lettering standing in for a specific culture.
southwest.referenceNote: These examples lean heavily toward Western poster imagery and desert travel. They are not representative of all Southwestern communities or artistic traditions.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

nautical.overview: A maritime-inspired vocabulary of clear markings, navigational structure, and restrained material cues. Decorative stripes are optional; the stronger idea is organized information.
steps: Use blue as a controlled accent
Make headings and units explicit
Use chart-like lines only when they communicate relationships
nautical.avoid: Fake coordinates, unexplained flag symbols, or ornamental compasses that look like controls.
nautical.example: A sailing journal with dated routes, weather observations, and clearly labeled maps.
nautical.typeAdvice: Use a sturdy sans-serif with clear numerals. Coordinates and measurements need consistent units and alignment.
nautical.referenceNote: Look at the maritime subjects, blue-and-cream combinations, and sailing imagery. A practical interface can borrow the organized markings without copying every decorative motif.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

rebus.overview: A visual word puzzle that substitutes pictures for words or syllables. Because its meaning depends on language and context, it is not a universal replacement for written labels.
steps: Use the puzzle as optional content
Provide a text equivalent or reveal
Keep navigation outside the puzzle
rebus.avoid: Replacing essential labels with ambiguous icons or assuming the same solution works across languages.
rebus.example: A puzzle page with a picture sequence, a labeled answer field, and an optional explanation.
rebus.typeAdvice: Use simple text around the symbols and an explicit text solution. Keep the puzzle's typography distinct from navigation.
rebus.referenceNote: The examples insert pictures into sentences and typographic layouts. Read the text and image together: the substitution depends on the specific language and phrasing.

timeMachine.classification: Editorial family: shared visual vocabulary, not a claim of common origin.

kawaii.overview: A reference to Japanese cute culture, expressed through compact forms, friendly characters, and playful detail. A cute appearance does not require childish language or a child audience.
steps: Use one consistent character language
Keep supporting labels plain
Make the character secondary to the task
kawaii.avoid: Infantilizing the reader, using emotion to pressure a decision, or letting decorative stickers obscure controls.
kawaii.example: A personal collection tracker with small character illustrations and clear item counts.
kawaii.typeAdvice: Rounded sans-serif titles can support compact characters. Keep body copy at ordinary reading sizes and use direct labels.
kawaii.referenceNote: The examples combine compact characters, sticker-like objects, and bright packaging compositions. Cute design can be saturated and busy; it is not restricted to pale pastels.
